head.title: Pyloxa — Use Claude Code and Codex together | Free Windows app
head.description: Free Windows app that splits coding work between Claude Code and Codex by your rules, checks each task with your own tests, and hands off when quota runs out.

why-title.2: Plenty of tools let you run several agents side by side. Pyloxa handles what happens between them: who does which part, how you know it is done, and who takes over when one gets stuck.

why-title.11: You decide what the agent in each terminal does; some tools also let an agent start helper agents.
why-title.12: The brain breaks the request into phases and tasks and routes each one by your rules, naming the rule it matched.
why-title.15: When one agent finishes, you paste the API shape and file paths into the next.
why-title.17: Agents can message each other; what gets handed over is up to the agents.
why-title.18: The next phase receives a handoff package: the results, the checks that passed, and what to watch for.
why-title.21: The agent says it is done, and you run the tests to find out.
why-title.23: You see which agents are working, done or waiting for you; whether the result is right is still yours to check.
why-title.24: A task is done when your verification commands pass in its own worktree. If they fail, the agent gets one automatic fix. You can also have a different agent write tests for it and the brain review it; the brain's verdict is labelled as an AI review.
why-title.27: You switch tools and explain again where things stand.
why-title.29: That terminal stops and waits; arranging a takeover is up to you.
why-title.30: Pyloxa proposes the fallback from your rules; once you confirm, it continues from the files the first agent changed.
why-title.33: The agent edits your working directory directly.

panel-rules.2: Rules match on phase type and task type, for example "backend work in the implementation phase goes to Codex backend". Each rule has a primary profile and a fallback order, and applies to every project or just the current one.
panel-rules.3: Rules are checked top to bottom and the first full match wins. Pyloxa warns you when one rule hides another.

panel-flow.1: Every phase is checked with your commands
panel-flow.2: The brain lays out phases to fit the request, such as specification, contract, implementation and testing. Before you approve, you can reassign a task, edit its instructions, or ask the brain to revise.
panel-flow.4: need your approval, and you can try them first in a temporary worktree. The brain can only use commands you approved.
panel-flow.5: Each finished task is checked in its own worktree; at the end of each phase, the gate runs again on the integrated result.
panel-flow.6: A gate can move on by itself once it passes, or wait for your approval.
panel-flow.7: Hand a finished task to a different agent to test it, for example Codex builds and Claude Code writes the tests. The tester can change only test files, and Pyloxa reruns your commands on the result.
panel-flow.8: The brain can review finished work, with its own model and thinking effort. Its verdict is labelled as an AI review, and a task that asks for your review still waits for you.

panel-modes.1: You decide how much to let go
panel-modes.2: The routing mode decides when Pyloxa asks you first. In every mode, pushing and deploying never happen on their own.

faq-title.3: Pyloxa is a desktop app for Windows 10 and 11 that gets AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex CLI to work together. You describe the work once, and the brain splits it into tasks and hands each one to a CLI by your routing rules. Every task runs in its own git worktree and is checked with your verification commands, and you decide what gets merged. If one CLI runs out of quota, another takes over once you confirm. Pyloxa uses your own subscriptions or API keys. The free edition is a direct download; Pro, coming soon at US$79 a year, adds running several projects at once, auto mode and automatic fallback.
faq-title.4: Does Pyloxa charge for AI usage?
faq-title.5: No. Pyloxa runs the official CLIs you already set up (Claude Code, Codex CLI and, experimentally, Gemini CLI), so usage counts against your own subscription, or against your own API key if you choose one. Pyloxa never resells or proxies any AI service.
faq-title.6: What do I need to install?
faq-title.7: Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit), git, and at least one of Claude Code or Codex CLI, signed in. Gemini CLI is optional and experimental, and needs your own paid Gemini API key. With more than one CLI, the default flow splits the work and fallback becomes useful. Don't have them yet? On first launch, the setup wizard checks for git and Node.js, installs the CLIs with their official npm commands after you confirm, and walks you through sign-in and API keys.
faq-title.9: Never. It checks sign-in status with each CLI’s own command and starts the CLI as you would. Tokens and credential files are not read, copied or sent.
faq-title.11: Pyloxa itself has no server and collects no telemetry. Your code goes only where the CLIs send it, under Anthropic’s, OpenAI’s and Google’s terms. Pyloxa asks GitHub for the latest Pyloxa version and its CLI compatibility catalog at startup and every 12 hours, with no project or usage data; you can turn this off in Settings. With Codex signed in, the usage meter also asks Codex CLI for your remaining usage every 10 minutes; Codex gets it from OpenAI with your own sign-in and uses no quota, and turning off the usage meter stops it. Usage statistics are computed on your computer and never sent.
faq-title.12: Can an agent break my repository?
faq-title.13: Agents work in separate git worktrees, away from the working directory you are editing, and Pyloxa never stashes, resets or checks it out. When a task finishes, its changed files are checked against the write scope the plan allows, and you can review each file in the built-in diff view. Nothing is merged or pushed until you choose to.
faq-title.14: Why does Windows warn me when installing?
faq-title.15: The free installer is not code-signed yet, so SmartScreen may say it protected your PC. Choose More info, then Run anyway. You can compare the installer’s SHA-256 with the one on the release page first.
faq-title.16: Can I choose the model and reasoning level?
faq-title.17: Yes. Each profile has its own model and reasoning setting, listed from the CLI you installed; leave them empty to use the CLI's defaults. The brain and the working agents can use different models.
faq-title.18: Can a kind of task always go to one agent?
faq-title.19: Yes. Write a routing rule, such as "testing-phase work goes to Claude Code", for every project or just this one. You can also reassign a single task before approving a plan. New installs start with a default flow: Claude Code for frontend and video, Codex for backend and images, Gemini for writing and docs. Change it any time.
faq-title.20: How is this different from tools that put agent terminals side by side?
faq-title.21: Terminal multiplexers put several agent terminals in one window so you can see which are working and which are waiting for you; some keep agents running even after you quit the app or reach remote machines. Pyloxa handles what happens outside the terminals: the brain splits the request into tasks, your rules route them, your commands check the results, a fallback is proposed when quota runs out, and you merge at the end. Pyloxa keeps working in the system tray when you close its window, and tasks interrupted by a restart can be resumed. If you want to watch every terminal yourself, a multiplexer fits; if you want to hand over a request and get checked results back, Pyloxa fits.
faq-title.22: I already pay for Claude or ChatGPT. Why not just run the CLI in a terminal?
faq-title.23: Running the CLI directly is fine, and Pyloxa uses the same CLI and the same subscription. The difference is three things: when quota runs out, Pyloxa proposes a fallback from your rules and, once you confirm, another CLI continues from the files already changed; an agent saying it is done does not count until your verification commands pass; and routing rules plus the skills each CLI can see are in one place instead of in each CLI's own settings.
faq-title.24: How is this different from a CLI's own subagents?
faq-title.25: Subagents split work inside one CLI. Pyloxa splits work across CLIs: tasks can go to different CLIs, each runs in its own worktree, your commands check the results, and another CLI takes over when one runs out of quota. You can use both together.
faq-title.26: Does it support Gemini or other agents?
faq-title.27: Since 0.1.2, Gemini CLI is supported as an experimental option with your own paid Gemini API key. Google account sign-in and AI Pro or Ultra subscriptions are not supported. Gemini can run tasks such as writing and docs but can’t be the brain or test another agent’s work, and in unattended mode it can edit files but not run commands. Other agents are being evaluated.
faq-title.29: The inventory is in the free version since 0.1.2: the Skills page lists the skills each CLI can read and flags skills that share a name but differ in content. Sync, per-project or per-profile assignment and routing packs are Pro and still in development; watch the release notes for the date.
faq-title.31: Several projects working at once with one inbox, automatic mode, automatic cross-testing by task type, an automatic fallback chain, and later quota scheduling and a shared skills library. Pro is US$79 a year. If you stop, Pro keeps working on every version released while you subscribed. Leave your email in the plans table for the early-bird price: US$49 a year, and it stays US$49 for as long as you stay subscribed. The free version stays free.
